content: Sulfiram, also known by its International Nonproprietary Name (INN) or as monosulfiram, is an ectoparasiticide primarily used for the treatment and prevention of scabies. It is commonly available in the form of a solution or as a medicated soap, and in some cases, it is combined with benzyl benzoate. Although its use has become infrequent, as of 2010, it remains available in certain countries such as Brazil, India, and South Africa as a monotherapy, and in France in combination with benzyl benzoate. Adverse effects associated with the use of sulfiram include dizziness, headache, fatigue, and the development of an erythematous rash. A single case of toxic epidermal necrolysis linked to sulfiram was reported in 1968. Structurally, sulfiram is related to disulfiram (commonly known as Antabuse) and undergoes rapid conversion to disulfiram when exposed to light. Similar to disulfiram, sulfiram can induce an unpleasant reaction when alcohol is consumed concurrently.
